In mathematics, a '''chiral algebra''' is an [[algebraic structure]] introduced by Beilinson and Drinfeld (2004)<ref>{{Cite book |last=Beilinson |first=Alexander |title=Chiral algebras |date=2004 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |others=Vladimir G. Drinfeld |isbn=978-0-8218-3528-9 |edition=Online-Ausg |series=Colloquium Publications |location=Providence, R.I}}</ref> as a rigorous version of the rather vague concept of a chiral algebra in physics. In Chiral Algebras, [[Alexander Beilinson|Beilinson]] and [[Drinfeld]] introduced the notion of chiral algebra, which based on the pseudo-tensor category of [[D-module]]s. They give a 'coordinate independent' notion of [[vertex algebra]]s, which are based on [[formal power series]]. Chiral algebras on curves are essentially [[vertex algebra#vertex operator algebra|conformal vertex algebra]]s.

== Definition ==
A '''chiral algebra'''<ref name="FBZ">{{cite book |last1=Ben-Zvi |first1=David |last2=Frenkel |first2=Edward |author-link2=Edward Frenkel |title=Vertex algebras and algebraic curves |date=2004 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |location=Providence, Rhode Island |isbn=9781470413156 |page=339 |edition=Second}}</ref> on a [[smoothness|smooth]] [[algebraic curve]] <math>X</math> is a [[Group action#Right group action|right]] D-module <math>\mathcal{A}</math>, equipped with a D-module [[homomorphism]]
<math display=block>\mu : \mathcal{A} \boxtimes \mathcal{A}(\infty \Delta) \rightarrow \Delta_! \mathcal{A}</math>
on <math>X^2</math> and with an [[embedding]] <math>\Omega \hookrightarrow \mathcal{A}</math>, satisfying the following conditions
* <math>\mu = -\sigma_{12} \circ \mu \circ \sigma_{12}</math> ([[Skew-symmetry]])
* <math>\mu_{1\{23\}} = \mu_{\{12\}3} + \mu_{2\{13\}}</math> ([[Jacobi identity]])
* The unit map is compatible with the homomorphism <math>\mu_\Omega: \Omega \boxtimes \Omega (\infty \Delta) \rightarrow \Delta_!\Omega</math>; that is, the following diagram commutes
<math display = block>
\begin{array}{lcl}
 & \Omega \boxtimes \mathcal{A}(\infty\Delta) & \rightarrow & \mathcal{A} \boxtimes \mathcal{A}(\infty \Delta) & \\
 & \downarrow && \downarrow \\
 & \Delta_!\mathcal A & \rightarrow & \Delta_! \mathcal A & \\
\end{array}
</math>
Where, for [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaves]] <math>\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N}</math> on <math>X</math>, the sheaf <math>\mathcal{M}\boxtimes\mathcal{N}(\infty \Delta)</math> is the sheaf on <math>X^2</math> whose sections are sections of the external tensor product <math>\mathcal{M}\boxtimes\mathcal{N}</math> with arbitrary poles on the diagonal:
<math display = block>\mathcal M \boxtimes \mathcal N (\infty \Delta) = \varinjlim \mathcal{M} \boxtimes \mathcal{N} (n \Delta),</math>
<math>\Omega</math> is the [[canonical bundle]], and the 'diagonal extension by delta-functions' <math>\Delta_!</math> is
<math display = block>\Delta_!\mathcal{M} = \frac{\Omega \boxtimes \mathcal{M}(\infty \Delta)}{\Omega \boxtimes \mathcal{M}}.</math>

== Relation to other algebras ==
=== Vertex algebra ===
The [[category (mathematics)|category]] of vertex algebras as defined by [[Richard Borcherds|Borcherds]] or [[Victor Kac|Kac]] is equivalent to the category of chiral algebras on <math>X = \mathbb{A}^1</math> equivariant with respect to the [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>T</math> of [[Translation (geometry)|translations]].

=== Factorization algebra ===
Chiral algebras can also be reformulated as [[factorization algebra]]s.
